entries.d: Boniface VIII made the largest claim to papal supremacy in the Church's history — and paid for it with a French king's soldiers breaking down his door. A brilliant canon lawyer who followed a pope who resigned, he opened the first Holy Year in 1300 to crowds beyond counting, then spent his final years locked in a ruinous fight with Philip IV of France that ended in his own humiliation. He died weeks later, a broken man, in a Church he had tried to make more powerful than any king.

sections.b: Benedetto Caetani was born around 1235 at Anagni, the son of Loffred Caetani, into a family originally of Spanish descent but long settled first at Gaeta and later at Anagni. He studied at Todi and Spoleto, likely also at Paris, and earned doctorates in both canon and civil law, becoming a canon successively at Anagni, Todi, Paris, Lyons, and Rome. In 1265 he accompanied Cardinal Ottobuono Fieschi to England on a mission to restore peace after the Second Barons' War, giving him early, direct experience of high diplomacy. Decades of service as a papal legate and canon lawyer followed, experience that made him, by the time of his election, one of the most formidable legal minds in Europe. Through his mother's family he was connected to the house of Segni, which had already given the Church three popes, including Innocent III, Gregory IX, and Alexander IV.

sections.h: The Pope After the Pope Who Resigned
sections.b: Boniface's predecessor, the hermit-pope Celestine V, had done something no pope had done in living memory: he resigned the papacy after only five months, unable to govern the office he had never sought. The cardinals elected Boniface in his place on 24 December 1294. Wary that Celestine might become a rallying figure for rivals who considered the resignation invalid, Boniface had the elderly former pope confined, where he died within the year — a decision that drew criticism at the time and has never fully escaped it since; Dante, writing a generation later, placed Boniface among the damned in the Inferno, in no small part because of it.

Whatever else divided contemporaries about him, Boniface's Holy Year of 1300 was an unqualified triumph: he proclaimed a plenary indulgence for any pilgrim who visited Rome's major basilicas, and the response — by contemporary accounts, hundreds of thousands of pilgrims over the year — filled the city's streets and its treasury alike and established a tradition of Jubilee years the Church still keeps. He also published the Liber Sextus, a major codification of canon law supplementing the Decretals of Gregory IX, which remained a standard reference for centuries. He founded what became Rome's Sapienza University in 1303, and was a significant patron of building and art in Rome and at Anagni, where the cathedral crypt still preserves frescoes and a marble throne associated with his reign.

sections.h: Unam Sanctam and the Outrage of Anagni
sections.b: Boniface's reign is remembered above all for its collision with King Philip IV of France. When Philip moved to tax the French clergy without papal consent, Boniface answered in 1296 with the bull Clericis Laicos, forbidding it. The conflict escalated for years and culminated on 18 November 1302 in Unam Sanctam, the single most absolute statement of papal supremacy any pope has ever issued, declaring it necessary for salvation that every human creature be subject to the Roman pontiff. Philip's response was not theological but physical: his minister Guillaume de Nogaret organized an armed raid on Boniface's palace at Anagni in September 1303. Soldiers broke in, reportedly struck or threatened the aged pope, and held him captive for several days before the townspeople of Anagni drove the raiders out and freed him.
Boniface returned to Rome, but the assault had shattered him — physically, and by most accounts psychologically as well. He died a little over a month later, on 11 October 1303.

Unam Sanctam remains the high-water mark of the papacy's claim to supreme authority over kings, a claim Boniface's own successor, Clement V, quietly softened within a few years under continued French pressure, formally assuring Philip IV that France had suffered no loss of standing because of it. The Outrage of Anagni is often read, in hindsight, as the moment the medieval papacy's temporal power began visibly to crack — a prelude to the Avignon Papacy that would soon follow, when the popes themselves came to live under the shadow of the French crown rather than in defiance of it. Dante's harsh judgment of Boniface in the Divine Comedy, written within a generation of his death, shows how quickly and how sharply even faithful Catholics turned on his memory. We do the man no favors by softening either half of that record: a pope of real learning, real reforming energy, and a genuinely popular Jubilee, and also a pontificate whose overreach and whose treatment of his own predecessor helped bring the medieval papacy's temporal ambitions to their breaking point.

quotes.text: It is altogether necessary for salvation for every human creature to be subject to the Roman pontiff.
quotes.source: Boniface VIII, Unam Sanctam, 1302

entries.d: No name in the long history of the papacy carries quite the weight of scandal that Alexander VI's does. Rodrigo Borgia rose through four decades of Church service before an election clouded by rumors of bribery, then spent eleven years advancing his own family with a boldness that shocked even a jaded Rome. He was also a real patron of Renaissance art and the pope whose bull divided the newly found Americas between Spain and Portugal. The Church has never pretended his conduct honored his office — only insisted, always, that his conduct was never the office itself.

sections.b: Rodrigo Borgia was born at Xàtiva, near Valencia in Spain, on 1 January 1431, to Jofre Llançol and Isabella de Borja. When his uncle, Isabella's brother Cardinal Alfonso de Borja, became Pope Callixtus III in 1455, the young Rodrigo's path was set: he was adopted into his uncle's household, took the Borgia name, and was sent to study law at the University of Bologna. At twenty-five he was made Cardinal-Deacon of San Nicola in Carcere; by twenty-seven he was already vice-chancellor of the Church, one of its most powerful administrative offices, a post he went on to hold under five successive popes — Callixtus III, Pius II, Paul II, Sixtus IV, and Innocent VIII — accumulating vast wealth and an unrivaled command of the papacy's inner workings across nearly four decades before his own election.

The 1492 conclave that elected him was close and contentious: Borgia won by a bare two-thirds majority, secured in part by his own vote. Contemporaries widely believed that simony — the buying of votes — played a role, a suspicion New Advent's own Catholic Encyclopedia calls "not improbable" even while noting it was never proven and the election stood as valid under the law of the time. He took the name Alexander VI and began his reign popular with the Roman people, launching building projects across the city.

Alexander was, in fact, a significant patron of the arts: he commissioned Pinturicchio to decorate the Borgia Apartments in the Vatican, and during his reign Bramante designed the elegant Tempietto on the traditional site of St. Peter's martyrdom. On the world stage, his most consequential act was the bull Inter Caetera of 1493, issued only months after Columbus's return from his first voyage, which divided newly discovered and yet-to-be-discovered lands in the Americas between Spain and Portugal — the basis for the later Treaty of Tordesillas, and a decision that shaped the colonial map of an entire hemisphere for centuries. He also navigated Italy's treacherous politics with real skill, and historians credit him with helping keep the invading French army of Charles VIII from establishing lasting control over the peninsula in 1494–1495.

None of this is what Alexander VI is remembered for. As a cardinal and then as pope he fathered several children — among them Cesare, Lucrezia, Juan, and Jofre — and advanced them with a boldness that shocked even a Rome accustomed to clerical concubinage and nepotism. Cesare Borgia became a ruthless political and military operator whom Machiavelli later studied closely as a model for The Prince; Lucrezia Borgia was married three times in succession to serve her father's shifting political alliances, each marriage dissolved or ended as the family's needs changed. Contemporary accounts, including the diary of Johann Burchard, the papal household's Master of Ceremonies, describe a papal court capable of real extravagance and scandal, most infamously the so-called Banquet of Chestnuts in 1501. Cesare Cantù, a nineteenth-century Catholic historian cited by New Advent, observed that by the mid-1800s Alexander VI was the one pope who had never found a Catholic apologist; a small number of later scholars have since argued that the very worst tales were exaggerated by political enemies and by writers such as Victor Hugo, but even the most sympathetic accounts do not deny the basic pattern of nepotism and personal corruption that defined his reign.

Alexander died at Rome on 18 August 1503, after a short and severe illness. Rumors that he had been poisoned — possibly by a plot of his own devising gone wrong — spread quickly through Rome and have circulated ever since, though no evidence has ever established it as fact.

Alexander VI is, by near-universal agreement, the most compromised man ever to hold the office of pope — a judgment Catholic historians themselves have made without flinching. His pontificate is a genuine argument for a distinction the Church has always insisted on: that the holiness of the Petrine office does not depend on the holiness of the man who happens, however unworthily, to occupy it. We tell Alexander's story honestly, not to excuse it, but because pretending it away would be its own kind of dishonesty — and because the doctrine his own life tested so severely is one the Church has held to regardless.

entries.d: History remembers him with two nicknames that don't obviously belong to the same man: the Warrior Pope, who led armies in the field and wore armor beneath his vestments, and the Renaissance Pope, whose patronage gave the world the Sistine Chapel ceiling. Giuliano della Rovere inherited a papacy the Borgias had left in ruins and rebuilt it through sheer force of will — political, military, and artistic all at once. The Church he left behind was stronger and infinitely more beautiful. It was also, in ways he could not have foreseen, closer than it had been in centuries to the crisis of the Reformation.

sections.b: Giuliano della Rovere was born on 5 December 1443 at Albissola, near Savona, to Raffaello della Rovere and Theodora Manerola, a family of probably noble but genuinely modest means. He entered the Franciscan Order, following his uncle Francesco della Rovere into religious life, and studied under his tutelage at Perugia. Everything changed when that uncle became Pope Sixtus IV in 1471: Giuliano was created Cardinal Priest of San Pietro in Vincoli within weeks, and was thereafter, in the words of one contemporary account, overwhelmed with benefices across Italy and France. He served as a papal legate on difficult diplomatic missions for decades, building a reputation as a capable, forceful operator. He was passed over for the papacy twice — in 1484, when Innocent VIII was elected, and in 1492, when he lost decisively to the far wealthier Rodrigo Borgia, an outcome he never fully forgave — before finally winning election unopposed on 1 November 1503, following the month-long reign of the elderly Pius III.

sections.h: A Papacy Weakened by the Borgias
sections.b: Julius inherited a Papal States badly depleted by Alexander VI's relentless promotion of his own family, particularly the military ambitions of Cesare Borgia, and an Italy caught in the wider Italian Wars between France, Spain, and the Holy Roman Empire for control of the peninsula. Restoring the Papal States to real strength became the defining project of his reign from its very first year.

Julius pursued that project on every front at once. He personally led military campaigns that recovered Perugia and Bologna for the Church in 1506–1507 and brought the Romagna back under papal control, then in 1508 joined the League of Cambrai, a coalition against an overreaching Venice, before reversing course in 1511 to form the Holy League against France instead — a sequence of alliances that shows how fluidly he was willing to maneuver to keep the Papal States intact. In 1506 he also founded the Swiss Guard, which still protects the pope today, and laid the cornerstone for an entirely new St. Peter's Basilica, commissioning the architect Donato Bramante to replace the ancient, crumbling original built more than a thousand years earlier by Constantine. He commissioned Michelangelo to paint the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel, a project carried out between 1508 and 1512 that the artist reportedly undertook reluctantly, preferring sculpture, and brought Raphael to Rome to fresco the papal apartments now known as the Raphael Rooms. In 1512 he convened the Fifth Lateran Council, and he ratified the Treaty of Tordesillas, formalizing the division of the New World his predecessor Alexander VI had set in motion.

None of Julius's contemporaries doubted that this was a pope who fought his own wars. He rode with his armies, oversaw sieges in person, and by several accounts wore armor beneath his papal vestments during campaigns, pursuing papal territorial claims with a single-mindedness that unsettled even hardened observers of Renaissance politics. He grew a beard, unusual and even irregular for a pope of his era, as a sign of mourning after the loss of Bologna in 1511, shaving it only shortly before his death. Machiavelli discussed him at length in The Prince, and many at the time, and many Catholic historians since, have found something genuinely troubling in a Vicar of Christ so thoroughly given to the sword rather than the shepherd's staff. His building projects, meanwhile, were financed in significant part through the sale of indulgences across northern Europe — the same fundraising practice that, within a few years of Julius's death, would give Martin Luther the specific grievance that opened the Reformation. Julius did not cause that crisis, but his pontificate, for all its artistic glory, is part of the kindling that made it possible.

Julius kept fighting almost to the end, forming the Holy League against France in 1511 even as his health declined. In October 1512 the Sistine Chapel ceiling was unveiled to the public for the first time, one of the last great triumphs of his reign. He died at Rome on the night of 20–21 February 1513.

Julius II left the papacy territorially secure and artistically unrivaled — the Sistine ceiling and the new St. Peter's alone would secure any pontiff's place in history. We remember him rightly for that patronage, and just as rightly for a militarism that even his own contemporaries considered ill-suited to his office, and for a method of financing his ambitions that helped set the stage for the greatest rupture Western Christianity has ever known. Few popes better illustrate how closely greatness and warning can sit side by side in a single reign.

entries.d: Thirteenth after Peter, Eleuterus led the Roman church for roughly fifteen years at the close of the second century, through a reign generous enough in peace that it left room for a real theological fight. A letter reached him from Christians facing torture and death in Gaul, carried in person by the young presbyter who would soon become one of the era's great theologians. What Eleuterus decided about the controversy they wrote to him about would help set the Church's course on prophecy and authority for centuries.

sections.b: Born in Nicopolis, in the Greek province of Epirus, Eleuterus had served as a deacon of the Roman church under Pope Anicetus and remained in that role under Anicetus's successor, Soter — a genuine clerical career, rare enough to be specifically recorded by his contemporary Hegesippus, that carried him to the papacy itself around the year 174.

Eleuterus's pontificate fell under the emperors Marcus Aurelius and, from 180, Commodus. While Christians elsewhere in the empire suffered real violence — the martyrdoms at Lyons in 177 remain one of the best-documented persecutions of the second century — Rome itself saw comparatively little bloodshed under his watch, and Commodus's reign brought Roman Christians something close to open peace.

In the aftermath of the Lyons persecution, the imprisoned confessors there wrote to Eleuterus about a controversial new movement spreading from Asia Minor: Montanism, which claimed continuing prophetic revelation through ecstatic trances. Their letter was carried to Rome by the presbyter Irenaeus, soon to become bishop of Lyons and one of the most important theologians of the early Church. Eleuterus, by the account of the Church Father Tertullian, was at first inclined to tolerate the movement before being persuaded to condemn it — a decision that helped settle, for the wider Church, that teaching authority rested with bishops in continuous succession from the Apostles, not with individual claims of new prophecy.

sections.h: A Legend of a British King
sections.b: Later medieval tradition, recorded in the Liber Pontificalis, holds that a British king named Lucius wrote to Eleuterus asking to be baptized a Christian. Most modern historians regard this story as legendary rather than historical — it appears centuries after Eleuterus's death and fits no other evidence for Christianity in Britain this early — though it remained influential in later English tradition.

Eleuterus is remembered chiefly for steering the Roman church through the Montanist controversy at a genuinely formative moment, helping establish that the authority to define Christian teaching belonged to the Church's bishops rather than to charismatic individual prophets, however sincere. He died, by the best modern reckoning, on 24 May 189, and was buried on the Vatican Hill among the earliest popes.

entries.d: No early pope's life reads less like a saint's legend and more like a real, difficult human story. Callistus I was, by his own harshest critic's account, once enslaved, then imprisoned for a financial scandal, then sent to the mines of Sardinia, before rising to become a bishop's most trusted advisor and finally pope himself — an election that split the Roman church for the first time in its history and left a rival calling himself bishop in defiance.

sections.h: A Slave, A Scandal, A Sentence
sections.b: Nearly everything known about Callistus's early life comes from Hippolytus's Philosophumena — a source written by a bitter theological rival, and so read with real caution, but one whose specific, checkable details have generally held up. As a young slave, Callistus was placed in charge of a bank handling other Christians' deposits; when the funds were lost, he tried to flee, was caught, and was sentenced to the treadmill. Freed through the intervention of fellow Christians hoping to recover some of the money, he then, by Hippolytus's account, provoked a public confrontation at a synagogue and was sentenced to the mines of Sardinia — a punishment that, whatever its exact justice, effectively made him a Christian confessor in the eyes of the Roman community.

sections.h: From Exile to the Pope's Right Hand
sections.b: When Marcia, the influential mistress of the emperor Commodus, secured the release of Christians condemned to the Sardinian mines, Pope Victor I deliberately left Callistus's name off the list of those to be freed; Callistus won his release anyway, falling at the feet of the freed men's escort and persuading him to include him regardless. Victor, displeased but unwilling to reverse the release, sent Callistus to live at Antium on a modest Church allowance rather than welcome him back to Rome. It was Victor's successor, Zephyrinus, who recalled Callistus, made him a deacon, and placed him in charge of the Christian burial ground that still bears his name today — a position of real trust that made Callistus, in effect, Zephyrinus's closest advisor for the rest of that pontificate.

sections.h: An Election That Split the Church
sections.b: When Zephyrinus died in 217, Callistus was elected by a majority of the Roman church to succeed him. Hippolytus, who considered Callistus's theology dangerously loose on questions surrounding the Trinity, refused to accept the outcome. He withdrew from communion with Callistus, gathered his own followers, and set himself up as a rival bishop of Rome — the city's first real schism, and one that would persist through two more of Callistus's successors before Hippolytus was finally reconciled.

Later tradition holds that Callistus died in a popular uprising in the Trastevere district of Rome, thrown from a window during a riot and his body cast into a well — an account that comes from sources written well after his death and cannot be fully verified, though it is consistent with the real hostility Callistus faced from some quarters, both pagan and Christian, during his pontificate. His crypt, decorated with paintings depicting this martyrdom, and a surviving piece of gold glass bearing his name and image, attest to how firmly this tradition took hold.

Callistus I is remembered both for real pastoral generosity — tradition credits him with relaxing several rigorist disciplinary rules and allowing greater flexibility in who the Church could readmit after serious sin — and for the schism his own election provoked, a genuine crack in Roman unity that took years to heal. Few early popes' lives illustrate so plainly that sanctity, in the Church's own reckoning, has never required a smooth or uncomplicated biography.
